one_liner: Tokio's docs-example TCP echo server on the single-threaded runtime; one 2022 run took 30.7 s against 43.6 s for the libuv docs example.
what_it_does: Tokio is Rust's dominant async runtime: a task scheduler, an I/O reactor over the OS event queue (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) and async TCP/UDP sockets. The measured program (benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct, 35 lines) is the README-style echo server: accept in a loop, tokio::spawn one task per connection, read into a 1 KiB stack array and write_all it back, under #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]. The Boost.Redis author wrote it as one of five echo servers driven by the same C++ Asio client. Using it from C++ means FFI or a separate Rust process; it is not a library you can link in place of libuv.
how_it_is_fast: Each connection is an async fn compiled to a stackless state machine whose 1 KiB buffer lives inside the task, so an echo costs one read and one write syscall and no heap allocation. Sockets are registered once with mio, which uses edge-triggered epoll (EPOLLET), and a read that hits WouldBlock parks the task until the reactor wakes it. The current-thread scheduler runs every task on one thread, so there is no work-stealing or cross-thread wake-up; it polls the I/O driver every 61 scheduled tasks (event_interval default in runtime/builder.rs). The libuv baseline makes the same syscalls but, as the unmodified docs example, mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer on each read callback (libuv passes 64 * 1024 as suggested_size) plus a write request per echo and frees both; how much of the 13 s gap that explains was never measured.
when_to_use: New network services in Rust with many concurrent, mostly idle connections exchanging small messages, where one task per connection is the simplest correct design.
Single-core or one-runtime-per-core deployments: the current_thread flavour is what produced the 30.7 s result; the default multi-thread runtime (tokio 0.2.25) took 42.2-43.2 s in the same harness.
When the C alternative under consideration is a straightforward libuv callback server written from the docs, without buffer pooling or request reuse.
As a sidecar or separate process next to C++ code when the team prefers Rust's ownership checks for network-facing parsing.
when_not_to_use: When C++ is an option: the Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server in the same chart took 29.5 s (October 2022) against Tokio's 30.7 s, and the July 2022 Asio run was 31.1 s, so the two are within noise of one single-run chart.

As proof that Rust or Tokio beats libuv: the libuv server allocates per message, was built with gcc -O2 against an unstated libuv, and was never revised, while the Tokio server was moved to a newer Tokio and the single-threaded runtime before its winning run.
Inside an existing C or C++ event loop: Tokio needs its own runtime thread and an FFI boundary; nothing in the benchmark covers that.

Handlers that block or burn CPU: on the current-thread scheduler every task shares one thread, so one blocking call stalls every connection, and in this harness the multi-thread runtime was slower, so moving off current_thread has a cost.
Latency-SLO work: only total wall time for 5,000,000 round trips exists, with no percentiles.

integration.dependencies: tokio (the benchmark enables features = ["full"]); tokio itself depends on mio for the OS event queue
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.85 for current Tokio (README MSRV); the benchmark's Cargo.lock pins tokio 1.20.0 (edition 2021); the rustc version and cargo profile used for the run are not stated
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll), macOS and BSD (kqueue), Windows (IOCP) per the Tokio README; measured only on the author's unnamed localhost machine
integration.thread_safety: current_thread runtime: all tasks are created and executed on the calling thread (runtime/mod.rs); the default multi-thread runtime is a work-stealing scheduler (README)

gotchas: The doc page's 'code used' link for Tokio points to commit 3fb018c, whose server is tokio 0.2.25 with the default multi-thread #[tokio::main] and scored 42.2 s (comment) and 43.2 s (chart), not the ab68e8a tokio 1.20.0 current_thread server behind the 30.7 s bar (2022-07-16, 'Updates to a more recent Tokio version and uses single thread.'). The version bump and the runtime switch happened together, so their effects cannot be separated.

The chart is a composite of single `time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000` runs from different dates: libuv 43.568 s by 2022-07-15, Tokio 2022-07-16, Go 2022-08-25, and Asio re-run at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07 after its server switched from io_context(1) to a typed executor with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO. On 2022-07-16 Tokio (30.7 s) was ahead of Asio (31.1 s); it was never re-run after Asio's tuning.

The single-threaded Asio client catches each session's exception, prints 'Error:' to stderr and carries on; it never checks that all 5,000,000 echoes completed or that the echoed bytes match, so a run with failed sessions would look faster. No logs of the runs are in the repository.

No hardware, OS, rustc version or cargo profile is given (the Cargo.toml has no [profile] section and no build command is documented), and the libuv build is gcc -O2 against a system libuv of unknown version; Tokio and Asio at about 30 s may both be capped by the single-threaded client on the same host (inferred, not measured).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the Go net echo server from the same harness (35.6 s), Tokio took about 14% less wall time and gives explicit control of the runtime flavour, so pick it when you want Rust's ownership model and are fine with async code. The Tokio 1M-task peak-memory entry (214 MB against 606 MB for concurrencpp and 853 MB for Asio) is the stronger reason to choose Tokio over a C++ coroutine runtime; this echo result alone is directional.
verified_claims_summary: One `time` run each of a single-threaded Boost.Asio client (1000 localhost connections x 5000 13-byte echoes) on the author's unnamed machine (localhost latency 0.07 ms) took 30.7 s against the Tokio 1.20.0 current_thread server and 43.6 s against the libuv docs example built with gcc -O2, about 1.42x less wall time (derived from page data). The Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine server took 29.5 s in a later run, Go 35.6 s and Node.js 74.2 s; no CPU, OS, rustc or libuv versions are given.
status_note: Tokio is actively maintained (MIT, 33.4k stars, README install snippet shows 1.53.2) and the server is a copyable docs example, but the evidence is a 2022 single-run composite chart that the current doc page still shows and links to the older Tokio code, against an allocation-heavy C example, so it supports only a tier-D directional claim.
